job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Felix Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for your time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do a master's in manufacturing engineering at Brandt Polytechnic, three days a week, and the other days I'm at my parents' machine shop in Kessler, where I still live. We make small steel parts for pumps and farm equipment. My dad, Ramon, has run the shop for twenty-six years, and my mum does the invoices.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do at the shop, and what do you make of your studies?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a milling machine, and I'm learning to program the newer one. My bachelor's in mechanical engineering was a pass, and I didn't do an internship because I was helping at the shop instead. I'd say the degree is fine, but I learn more by standing at the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, no change. I'd tell my dad it's what he always said: the shiny new thing arrives, and the work stays the same. I wouldn't post anything online, because I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan stays put. I finish the master's, work at the shop and maybe take a job at a bigger factory for a few years to learn how a proper line is run. My parents' money covers the fees, and I have over six months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the three days at the shop and the three days at university. I'd apply to two or three manufacturers near Kessler, like Hartman Gears, for a graduate post next spring. I'd also fix the old lathe, since it's been rattling for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like normal life, and I like normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a normal year look like for the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A normal year is orders from the same six customers, a slow February, a busy October and one machine that breaks at the worst time. If AI is only hype, we still have to fix that machine with a spanner. I think about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you picture running the shop yourself one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One day, maybe. Dad hasn't said it, and I haven't either. I'd rather learn on a big line first, so I come back with something my dad doesn't know.

say: I'd tell my dad it's what he always said: the shiny new thing **arrives** and the work stays.
I wouldn't post anything online, because I **don't**.
think: My plan stays put: finish the master's and work at the **shop**.
A few years at a **bigger factory** would teach me how a proper line runs.
do: Keep three days at the shop and three days at **university**.
Apply to two or three manufacturers like Hartman Gears and fix the old **lathe**.
feel: **Calm**. It feels like normal life, and I like normal.
S0.quote: I'd rather learn on a big line first, so I come back with something my dad doesn't know.
fieldNote: Content with the **familiar**: he treats a quiet world as simply more of his own routine.
Quietly hopes to **inherit** the shop but hasn't said so to his father.

steps.text: Keep three days at the shop and three at university
Apply to Hartman Gears for a graduate post next spring
Repair the old lathe in the winter break

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, let's see what's real and not run around. I'd tell my friends it's too early to quit anything. I'd talk to my dad's customers, the ones who send drawings, to see whether they want anything different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the desk side of the shop goes first: quoting, drawings, scheduling and the invoices my mum does. The machines stay for a long time. But a pass degree for a desk job is a weak card, so I lean on the machine side. It's a bit of an advantage that I'm hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my mum to try the quoting software a supplier is pushing, and I'd sit with her to see if it works. I'd learn the new CNC controller properly, since that's the part where tools come in. I'd cut a few costs, like my gym and the car upgrade I planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job isn't in danger, but the shop's paperwork and the graduate market both feel shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the shop's tasks would software take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Some of the design work I'd get at a big firm would be done by software by then, so I'd have fewer places to start. I haven't touched it because I dislike things that give answers without showing the working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools. Is that a problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might be, but I'd rather learn on the shop's own jobs than on something abstract. If I use it, it's for quoting, since a bad quote costs us money and I'd see the mistake at once.

say: Let's see what's real and **not run around**.
I'd ask my dad's customers whether they want anything **different**.
think: The **desk side** of the shop goes first: quoting, drawings, scheduling and invoices.
A pass degree is a weak card for desk jobs, so I lean on the **machines**.
do: Sit with my mum and test the **quoting software** a supplier is pushing.
Learn the new **CNC controller** properly and cut a few costs.
feel: **Uneasy**: my job isn't in danger, but the paperwork and graduate market feel shaky.
S1.quote: I dislike things that give answers without showing the working.
fieldNote: His resistance is **principled**, not lazy: he distrusts tools that hide their working.
Sees the risk in the **office side** of the family firm, and handles it by asking his mother to test one tool.

steps.text: Test the supplier's quoting software with my mum
Learn the new CNC controller properly
Cut the gym membership and drop the car upgrade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, calm down, but I'd say it more to myself. At work I'd ask the customers what they'd do. Online I wouldn't say anything, but I'd go to a town meeting about it, because that's where people in Kessler would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be scared for the shop. If AI can do all the planning by 2028 and robots can run the machines by 2031, the shop's value drops. Dad's clients might buy cheaper parts from a robot factory. I'd also wonder if my degree is worth what he paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the master's if it didn't pay off. Not at once, but I'd ask my professor what's useful. I'd talk to Dad about getting a quote for a robot cell, because if it's coming, I'd rather own one than get run over by it. I'd also move savings into a plain bank account and not buy the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't panic, but my jaw is tight all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Dad, we need to decide whether to be the shop that buys the robot or the shop that gets bought. He'd say, we've survived before. But that was against another shop, not against a machine that doesn't tire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still do the master's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, but I'd change the topic of my thesis to automation and robot cells for small shops. If I'm going to be scared, I may as well know what I'm scared of.

say: Calm down, I'd say, but more to **myself**.
I'd go to a **town meeting** in Kessler, because that's where people would be.
think: If robots run the machines by 2031, the shop's **value drops**.
I'd wonder if my degree is **worth** what my parents paid.
do: Ask a supplier for a **quote** on a robot cell for the shop.
Move savings into a plain bank account and **skip the car**.
feel: Anxious: I don't panic, but my **jaw** is tight all day.
S2.quote: We need to decide whether to be the shop that buys the robot or the shop that gets bought.
fieldNote: The fear is for the **family business**, and he responds by proposing an investment to his father.
His 'resistant' side shows in **no AI tools**, while he still considers a robot cell.

steps.text: Get a quote for a robot cell from the machine supplier
Move savings into a plain bank account
Change the thesis topic to robot cells for small shops
Go to the town meeting about the shop's future

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, but not enough to be relaxed. I'd tell my friends to start learning a second thing. At the shop I'd tell my father we should write down every job we do and how much each earns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's slower to hit, and I'd have a few years of working before the thinking AI arrives. But the robots around 2034 are aimed at exactly what my dad's shop does. I'd be late twenties, with a shop that might not make sense by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work at the shop and at the bigger firm, and save most of what I earn. I'd get one robot cell for the shop when we can afford it, paid mostly from savings, rather than wait. I'd also learn how to program it, which is the first thing I'd do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan, which helps. I don't sleep badly. I just think a lot while driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me do things in the right order. With two years I'd be guessing. With five I'd be making choices. I'd learn how the newer kit runs, then decide what to buy, instead of buying in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your dad's shop in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it going and get it ready for the change. Our customers value quality and quick turnaround, and I think a small shop with one robot cell can do that. If it fails, then we sell the machines while they still have a price.

say: We've got time, but **not enough to relax**.
I'd tell my father to write down every job and how much each **earns**.
think: The thinking AI arrives later, but robots around 2034 are aimed at **what the shop does**.
By my late twenties the shop might not **make sense**.
do: Save most of what I earn and buy one **robot cell** when we can afford it.
feel: Anxious, but with a **plan**, which helps.
S3.quote: Five years lets me do things in the right order. With two years I'd be guessing. With five I'd be making choices.
fieldNote: Time converts his anxiety into an **ordered plan**: learn, decide, buy, in that order.
Plans an **exit date** for the shop's machines if the robot cell fails, a hard-headed touch.

steps.text: Write down every shop job and what each earns
Save most of my earnings towards a robot cell
Buy one robot cell and program it myself
Learn the cell's programming through the supplier's course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and I'd be glad to have it. I'd tell friends that nothing's decided and not to wreck their plans. I'd want to hear what my father thinks, since he's seen more cycles than I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit uneasy, but not scared. By 2036 I'd be thirty-four, with a decade of experience, maybe running the shop. Robots arrive in 2039, so I'd have time to build something that gets the work done differently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work at a bigger factory for three years, and then come back to the shop. I'd buy the first robot cell when it makes sense and keep a few older machines. I'd also learn to use the AI tools at last, slowly, once I see which ones the big factory uses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but fine. A decade is long enough that I stop thinking about it most weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First two years, I'd finish the degree and take the factory job. Dad would run the shop. I'd come home on Saturdays to work the mill, so I don't lose the feel. The factory teaches me how tasks get measured and planned, and that's what I'd bring back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger apprentices at your dad's shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the apprentices to learn the machine and the numbers. If you only know one, you're stuck when the other one changes. Our apprentice Dani is eighteen and asks smart questions, and I'd keep encouraging that.

I'd tell friends **nothing's decided**, so don't wreck your plans.

fieldNote: With ten years his **conservatism** becomes a sequence: factory first, shop second, tools last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. The shop is my family's whole income, and a machine that doesn't tire could undercut my dad before I'm ready. What would help is cheap loans to small workshops that want to buy automation, and clear warning from the suppliers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against new things. I just want to see how they work before I put the family's money on them.

headlineQuote: I'm not against new things. I just want to see how they work before I put the family's money on them.
portrait: Felix is a **24-year-old** manufacturing master's student who works at his parents' machine shop in Kessler.
He passed his degree without internships, and he **never uses AI tools**, since he distrusts hidden working.
He is centre and resistant: he plans in **sequence**, learns first, decides second and buys last.
His mood moves from calm to **anxious** because the shop is his family's whole income.
He copes with savings, a possible **robot cell** and a stint at a bigger factory.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because a machine that doesn't tire could undercut his father's shop before he's ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small workshops to buy automation, and clear warning from suppliers.
